query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of Zr to a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy will improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance by enhancing solid-solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of Zr (e.g., 0.05 atomic fraction) to the alloy
generation.conditions: Vacuum induction melting or other suitable processing methods; testing in various environments, including room temperature, high temperature, and corrosive media
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Ni7Zr2 intermetallic compounds and Zr-rich phases
generation.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening due to the addition of Zr, which hinders grain boundary sliding and dislocation motion, leading to improved mechanical properties and corrosion resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved hardness, compressive strength, and corrosion resistance, as well as enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance, compared to the as-processed baseline alloy
generation.baseline: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without Zr addition
generation.boundary: Alloy composition, processing conditions, and testing environments
generation.uncertainty: Optimal amount of Zr addition, potential effects of Zr on phase stability and microstructure evolution, and interactions with other alloying elements

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with varying amounts of Zr (e.g., 0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 atomic fraction); process the alloys using vacuum induction melting or other suitable methods; test the alloys in various environments, including room temperature, high temperature, and corrosive media; measure mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, compressive strength), corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Zr does not lead to significant improvements in mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified
